<article class="paper-record">
<p class="paper-authors"><span class="paper-author me">Honglin Li</span>, <span class="paper-author">Buxin She</span>, <span class="paper-author">Jie Zhang</span></p>
<p class="paper-venue"><em>Energy Conversion and Management</em>, vol. 372, article 122376, 2027.</p>
<section aria-labelledby="abstract"><h2 id="abstract">Abstract</h2>
<p class="paper-abstract">Growing data-center electricity demand has increased interest in colocation with small modular reactors, but the conditions under which reactor power and steam-driven cooling reduce energy costs remain uncertain. Cooling can account for 20%–40% of facility electricity use, making steam extraction a potential source of savings as well as a loss of turbine generation. We co-optimize hourly reactor dispatch, steam extraction, absorption cooling and grid exchange for a 200 MWₑ data center in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region, using a 109-entry scenario set spanning capital, market, policy, financing and cooling efficiency. At 2023 mid-range reactor capital, the nuclear configurations cost 54.9%–67.7% more than grid supply even with the Section 45Y production tax credit. With the other 2023 assumptions held fixed, cogeneration reaches grid parity near $5000 kWₑ⁻¹. At nth-of-a-kind capital, nuclear supply is 85.9%–98.7% cheaper than grid procurement in 2023, but between parity and 34.8% more expensive in the low-price 2024 market. A carbon price of $53.1–64.0 tCO₂⁻¹ closes the mid-range gap when exports receive credits at the hourly average grid emission factor; the resulting negative balances are attributional and do not represent physical carbon removal. Absorption cooling responds to hourly electricity prices and supplies 32.6% of annual cooling, but adds $9.7 million yr⁻¹ relative to the reactor-only plant. Absorption breaks even at an installed cost of $26 kW<sub>c</sub>⁻¹ at baseline efficiency and $529 kW<sub>c</sub>⁻¹ on a legacy-efficiency campus, compared with surveyed commercial prices of $450–1200 kW<sub>c</sub>⁻¹. Within the tested ranges, reactor capital and market conditions have the largest effects on competitiveness, while the value of heat recovery depends on absorber cost and the efficiency of the electric cooling it replaces.</p>
<p class="paper-source">Abstract source: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enconman.2026.122376">Abstract of the published article, Energy Conversion and Management 372 (2027) 122376</a>.</p></section>
